newsitem.title: GERMANY: Budget crisis drives wedge into German coalition.
newsitem.headline: Budget crisis drives wedge into German coalition.

text.p: The yawning budget gap threatening Germany's ability to qualify for Europe's single currency began on Sunday to put strain on the weakest link in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition -- taxation.
As Finance Minister Theo Waigel scrambled to cut the deficit with very un-German methods, pressure mounted from his own colleagues simply to raise fuel or value-added tax.

While economic experts continued to attack Waigel's desperate attempts to raise money by revaluing gold reserves or selling shareholdings, his Free Democrat coalition partners made clear their determination to block higher taxes.

"There must be no tax increases to plug gaps in the budget," Free Democrat (FDP) general secretary Guido Westerwelle told national ZDF television on Sunday, defending a policy on which the FDP has staked its political survival.

But a groundswell of opinion within Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and their sister party, Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), is demanding action from a government looking increasingly panicky since news last week that tax revenues will be a huge 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) below budget this year.

Udo Ludwig, director of the Halle Economic Institute, one of Germany's "big six" institutes, said Waigel's proposals to revalue central bank currency and gold reserves were window dressing that used up some of Germany's most valuable resources.
Heiner Flassbeck, head of the Economic Research Institute in Berlin, told the weekly Bild am Sonntag that Waigel's plan undermined Germany's credibility with its European partners.
"Waigel has always claimed to be a paragon of correctness. Now it turns out he preaches water but drinks wine," he said.

Bonn has committed itself so strongly to iron budget discipline for itself and its European Union partners that a deficit above the limit set to qualify for monetary union to start in 1999 is almost unthinkable.
But this means Waigel has to find more money in time to meet the criteria this year.

CDU/CSU members of parliament last week applauded a young CDU member, Juergen Augustinowitz, who dared to suggest that a cut in the "solidarity tax" -- already deferred once in a humiliating blow to the FDP -- should be postponed again.
The income tax surcharge is intended to pay for the reconstruction of east Germany's economy.
CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble was reported to have told Augustinowitz: "We can come back to the idea in June".
This might prevent a damaging revolt against higher taxes at an FDP party conference next weekend.
"We have to sit down with the FDP leaders after the congress to decide how to put off the cut in the solidarity tax," Rainer Eppelmann, head of the CDU's labour wing, told Bild am Sonntag.
But Baden-Wuerttemberg state finance minister Walter Doering of the FDP highlighted the problem for Kohl and for the FDP, which has narrowed its focus to the single issue of tax cuts.
"The very existence of the FDP is linked to not raising fuel tax, as some CDU deputies want, and to cutting the solidarity surcharge," Doering told the Berliner Morgenpost daily.
Kohl needs the FDP to maintain his 12-seat parliamentary majority in the current parliament.
If the FDP's credibility is hurt again, its share of the vote in the September 1998 election could slip below the five percent it needs to return to parliament, depriving Kohl of his majority.
"Our coalition partner isn't exactly making life easy for us," Welt am Sonntag quoted Kohl as telling his parliamentarians.
But the risk of dancing to the FDP tune may be just as big.

"The government finds itself caught in a tax trap laid by the FDP. Falling public revenues and limits on new borrowing are robbing it of any possibility of shaping policy," wrote the daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung. ($ = 1.692 German Marks)
